prompt: An online store's product pages are viewed millions of times a day, but product details change only a few times a week. Each page shows the shopper's personalized price, and loads must stay under 50 ms.
tells: viewed millions of times a day
change only a few times a week
why: Read-heavy, rarely changing and latency-critical: put an in-memory cache in front of the database and invalidate it when a product is edited.
trap: A CDN only works when the whole page is the same for everyone. Personalized prices make the page dynamic, but the product data underneath can still be cached.

prompt: Every API request has to look up the caller's session. Sessions live in a SQL database that is starting to buckle, though they rarely change after login.
why: A tiny key-value lookup repeated on every request belongs in memory (for example Redis), not on a disk-backed database.
trap: Replicas would spread the load, but each lookup still costs a database round trip. A lookup this hot and this small is what a cache is for.

prompt: A leaderboard is computed by a heavy query that takes 4 seconds. Thousands of users open it, and it's fine if the numbers are up to a minute old.
tells: fine if the numbers are up to a minute old
why: Expensive to compute + staleness allowed: cache the result with a ~60 s TTL so the query runs once a minute, not thousands of times.
trap: Replicas would just run the 4-second query thousands of times on more machines.

prompt: One celebrity's profile gets 200k reads per second whenever they post, while most profiles get a handful.
why: A single hot key. Cache it, even in each server's own memory, so the spike never reaches the database.
trap: Sharding spreads different keys across machines, but one hot key still lands on one shard.

prompt: Your service calls a third-party geocoding API that charges per request. The same addresses are looked up over and over.
tells: same addresses are looked up over and over
why: Identical lookups repeated over and over: store each response keyed by its address and stop paying for repeats.
trap: Rate limiting caps your spend by refusing work. A cache avoids paying for work you've already done.

prompt: Hundreds of services read feature flags on every request. Flags change a few times a day, and a short delay before changes apply is acceptable.
tells: read feature flags on every request
short delay before changes apply is acceptable
why: Each service keeps a local cache with a short TTL. The tolerated delay is the TTL.
trap: Pushing changes over a queue works too, but reads on every request plus an acceptable delay is the cache signature.

prompt: Rendering a profile card means stitching together data from five microservices, which takes 800 ms. Profiles are viewed far more often than they're edited.
tells: viewed far more often than they're edited
why: Cache the assembled card and invalidate it when the profile is edited, so the 800 ms cost is paid once per edit, not once per view.
trap: Replicas would need adding to all five services and would still pay the stitching cost on every view.

prompt: Shopping carts are read on every page and updated a few times per visit. Reads must be fast, and the cart must never show stale items after an update.
tells: never show stale items after an update
why: A write-through cache updates the cache on every write, so reads are fast and never stale.
trap: Read replicas lag behind the primary, so an item the shopper just added can briefly vanish.
